newsitem.title: VIETNAM: FEATURE - U.S. left dilapidated nuclear legacy in Vietnam.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - U.S. left dilapidated nuclear legacy in Vietnam.

text.p: Deep in the highlands of southern Vietnam, on a hill above this picturesque honeymoon resort, lies a sinister and dilapidated remnant of the Cold War.
To outward appearances all that is visible is a rusting U.S.-built collection of space-age buildings with peeling paint behind a wire fence and set in concentric circles around a humming inner core.
The complex is partly overgrown by grass, flanked by a couple of near-derelict sheds and guarded at its main entrance by a lone policeman.

It's no place for the environmentally faint-hearted. This is Vietnam's Atomic Research Centre, complete with a reactor left here courtesy of a mid-century U.S. vision of supplying its wartime Saigon ally with the dangerous technology of clean, limitless power.
Now, 22 years after the Vietnam war ended, this forgotten problem is back in the news again.

In early January Washington officials unveiled classified documents detailing a bungled U.S. covert operation in March 1975 which resulted in a chunk of deadly plutonium being left at the plant at the war's end and falling into Hanoi's hands.

Two secret operatives, sent to Dalat as South Vietnam was collapsing around them, mistook a grey canister at the plant containing a relatively harmless alloy of pollonium and beryllium for the plutonium.

By the time the mistake was discovered they were gone, with the wrong canister, and this colonial hill station had fallen into enemy hands. Today, say the plant officials, the plutonium is still here.
SAFETY FEARS DISMISSED

"We have respected very strictly the provisions of the nuclear non-proliferation treaty," says Tran Ha Anh, the institute's French-educated director, dismissing what he calls exaggerated Western media reports over the matter.
"Frankly speaking we have other things to do. We have other problems to think about in Vietnam than making a bomb."
No one seriously accuses Vietnam of harbouring any sinister nuclear ambitions, but the amount of plutonium involved is in dispute.
U.S. officials say it is 80 grams (about three ounces) and have asked International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) inspectors to verify this. Vietnamese experts including Anh say the amount is less.
In either case it is not enough to make a bomb, and in recent weeks officials at the institute have made unusual efforts at candour to show foreign journalists what is involved.
As a TV camera whirs a technician in a lemon-yellow hospital gown uses rusty scissors to prise open a grey stainless steel container locked in a barely guarded outhouse.
Wearing nothing more than plastic gloves, he pulls out a glass cork to reveal what we are told is a radioactive lump.
"This is the American plutonium," a plant official says, standing back. "It's radioactive, but don't worry. It's all right to be exposed to it for a short time."
REACTOR IS JUST FOR PEACEFUL RESEARCH

Since the war the reactor has been reactivated and re-equipped using Soviet and IAEA help. Once a month it is fired into life for research purposes that cover areas including medicine and pollution control.
"Nuclear power programme research is the main objective," says Anh. "We are preparing for a nuclear power plant in Vietnam by 2010 to 2015."
But if this is a vision of future energy ambitions for one of the world's poorest countries, it does little to instil confidence.
As the reactor comes alive a series of alarms ring out. Officials say their safety record is excellent, but leukaemia is known to have afflicted at least one senior scientist here.
According to officials here a worker connected with Vietnam's nuclear programme in Hanoi was also injured in an accident involving a microtron accelerator.

Nonetheless after a brief flurry of publicly aired debate in the early 1990s, government officials seem intent on pursuing the goal of bringing Vietnam into the fold of Asian nations which see nuclear power as the answer to their energy needs.

Concerns raised as recently as 1995 over the problems of nuclear waste, financing and technology, have given way to an apparent determination to see nuclear energy as the answer to maintaining Vietnam's continued economic growth.
"We're always willing to participate with other countries in our nuclear research," says Anh. "IAEA and even U.S. experts want to come here. We're open to such a mission."
